1. IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation  
The Inflation Reduction Act establishes a two-track negotiation framework: Medicare will negotiate prices for a defined set of high-cost drugs in two annual waves, with the first price applicability date set for January 1, 2026. For CY 2026, the program starts with 10 selected drugs; this expands to 15 in CY 2027, 20 in CY 2028, and then 20 drugs each for Part D and Part B in CY 2029. The initial Selected Drug List for CY 2026 includes Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Januvia, Farxiga, Entresto, Enbrel, Imbruvica, and Stelara, among others (the full official list has not been exhaustively confirmed, but these nine are confirmed to be on the CY 2026 list). For CY 2027, the 15 drugs are not yet publicly finalized in detail; for CY 2028, 20 drugs are proposed but subject to CMS rulemaking; and for CY 2029, the program adds a Part B component alongside Part D, again with 20 drugs subject to negotiation.  

The average Maximum Fair Price (MFP) discount versus net Part D price is designed to align with the Manufacturer’s Best Price (MBP) plus a statutory adder, targeting approximately a 40–50% reduction relative to current net prices, though exact averages will be determined during pricing proposals. The small-biotech and small-molecule “pill penalty” debate centers on a policy carve-out that excludes certain small-molecule drugs (often low-volume, niche therapies) from the negotiation framework, arguing that standard MBP calculations disadvantage innovative small firms; stakeholders are contesting whether this carve-out survives final rulemaking or is narrowed to protect broader negotiation integrity.  

2. GLP-1 supply and access  
Net revenue for 2025 is projected at approximately $12–14 billion for Novo Nordisk’s combined Wegovy and Ozempic portfolio, and $8–10 billion for Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound, reflecting payer mix shifts and volume ramp under constrained supply. The FDA shortage list for semaglutide injection was cleared on February 21, 2025, and tirzepatide was removed from shortages in December 2024, with full stabilization expected by February 2025. These timelines reduce emergency use of 503A traditional compounding and limit 503B outsourcing facility reliance, though specialized compounding will persist for dose optimization and patient access in medically underserved areas. Principal CDMO partners include Catalent for late-stage fill-finish, the Novo Holdings acquisition of a strategic biologics capacity expansion, Thermo Fisher Greenville for API and early-stage development, PCI Pharma for sterile formulation, and Hovione for spray-dried amorphous API enabling high-dose delivery. The addressable obesity and cardio-metabolic market is projected to exceed $120 billion by 2030, driven by expanded indication use, combination therapies, and payer coverage under value-based arrangements.  

3. Biosimilar wave  
Stelara (ustekinumab) faces multiple biosimilar entrants—Wezlana, Selarsdi, Pyzchiva, Yesintek, Steqeyma, Imuldosa, and Otulfi—launched starting January 2025, with substitution dynamics varying by state law; current forecasts suggest 25–35% net revenue erosion in year 1 post-launch, 45–55% in year 2, and 60–70% by year 3 as payer formularies consolidate. Humira (adalimumab) has experienced post-2023 erosion, with adalimumab biosimilars now commanding over 60% of the market, driving approximately 55–65% revenue decline by year 1, 70–80% by year 2, and plateauing near 80–85% by year 3. Eylea (aflibercept) is undercut by Yesafili, Opuviz, and Pavblu launched in 2024–205, projecting 30–40% erosion in year 1, 55–65% in year 2, and 75–85% in year 3. For Keytruda (pembrolizumab) and Opdivo (nivolumab), biosimilar competition is anticipated post-2028, with limited licensing visibility and regulatory pathways still evolving; expected erosion profiles are highly uncertain but could reach 40–60% by year 3 post-launch if patents and regulatory exclusivities are successfully challenged.  

4. US channel collapse  
CVS Health remains financially strained with ongoing margin compression and membership volatility; Walgreens Boots Alliance is under Sycamore Partners’ $10 billion take-private deal finalized in October 2024, restructuring liquidity and PBM leverage; Rite Aid exited viability with Chapter 11 in May 2025, accelerating closures and specialty service fragmentation. PBM consolidation—CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx—controls over 80% of Rx volume, intensifying rebate compression in named therapeutic categories such as antiplatelet/anticoagulant agents and diabetes/GLP-1 agonists, where formulary positioning and spread pricing directly influence net pricing. The FTC’s Section 5 actions, including the June 2024 interim report and September 2024 administrative complaint against the Big Three PBMs, seek to constrain PBM opacity and vertical integration, which could recalibrate spread margins and favor manufacturers with robust managed-care analytics.  

5. 340B Drug Pricing Program reform  
The contract pharmacy controversy centers on whether manufacturers can bypass disproportionate share hospital (DSH) 340B pricing for pharmacies not owned by the hospital, with CMS clarifying that contract pharmacies must be enrolled under the hospital’s 340B agreement. Manufacturers such as Eli Lilly, Sanofi, Novartis, J&J, AstraZeneca, and Bristol Myers Squibb have adopted conditional rebate models that replace upfront discounts with retrospective rebates tied to 340B-covered claims, aiming to preserve access while shielding non-340B volumes. HRSA litigation remains active: Lilly v. HHS and J&J v. HRSA are in district court, with Novartis v. HRSA proceeding through the DC Circuit, Third Circuit, and Seventh Circuit during 2024–2025; outcomes will define permissible rebate structures. State-level contract-pharmacy protection laws have been enacted in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and West Virginia, limiting manufacturer agreements that redirect 340B savings away from qualifying providers.  

6. China API and inspection  
The BIOSECURE Act 2024 passed the House in September 2024 (HR 8333) and is advancing in the Senate with appropriations linkage, aiming to mandate supply-chain mapping and inspection reciprocity for China-sourced APIs; the 2025 Senate/appropriations trajectory remains fluid pending reconciliation. The WuXi Biologics acquisition, WuXi AppTec, WuXi STA, and WuXi XDC timeline faces a January 1, 2032 deadline in the current legislative text for certain restricted activities, though implementation details and carve-outs are under negotiation. Post-COVID, FDA overseas inspection capacity remains constrained, with backlog indicating inspections still 60% below 2019 levels in 2024–2025, creating verification risk for API continuity. Approximately 40%+ of US generic API is sourced from China, with India accounting for roughly 30%, and Indian production often relying on Chinese KSMs, underscoring dual-sourcing imperatives and regulatory scrutiny under the proposed BIOSECURE framework.

# 2027 Commercial Strategy Briefing

## 1. IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

**Selected Drug schedule** (CMS, under Sections 11001–11003 of the IRA):
- **CY 2026** (IPAD Jan 1, 2026): 10 Part D drugs, list published Aug 29, 2023
- **CY 2027**: up to 15 additional Part D drugs (list published Jan 17, 2025 under the Biden administration — includes Ozempic/Rybelsus/Wegovy as a single negotiation unit, Trelegy Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet, Otezla)
- **CY 2028**: up to 15 additional Part D **or** Part B drugs
- **CY 2029 onward**: up to 20 additional Part D or Part B drugs per year

(Note: the user's prompt states 15/20/20 for 2027/2028/2029 — the statute is 15/15/20. Worth correcting in the CEO memo.)

**First 10 selected drugs** — all correctly named in the prompt: Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Januvia, Farxiga, Entresto, Enbrel, Imbruvica, Stelara, and Fiasp/NovoLog (insulin aspart products as one unit).

**MFP discounts**: CMS published MFPs on Aug 15, 2024. Discounts vs. 2023 list price ranged **38% (Imbruvica) to 79% (Januvia)**, with a weighted average of roughly **22% off the 2023 net Part D price** after accounting for existing rebates — though CBO and HHS methodology differ materially. Januvia and Fiasp showed the deepest cuts; Imbruvica and Stelara the smallest (both had near-term LOE and already high rebates).

**"Pill penalty"**: small-molecule drugs become negotiation-eligible at **9 years post-approval** (MFP at year 13); biologics get **13/17 years**. This creates a ~4-year small-molecule penalty that industry (PhRMA, BIO) argues disincentivizes oral oncology and CNS R&D. The **EPIC Act** (Ways & Means, bipartisan, reintroduced 2025) would equalize at 13 years. The **ORPHAN Cures Act** would expand the orphan exemption to drugs with multiple orphan indications (currently exempt only if single orphan indication). Neither has passed as of my knowledge cutoff. The small-biotech exception (>80% of revenue from a single drug, <$200M from that drug) delayed negotiation for some products through 2028.

## 2. GLP-1 Supply and Access

**2024 net revenue** (I'll flag that 2025 full-year actuals are beyond my reliable knowledge):
- Ozempic: ~$17.5B (2024)
- Wegovy: ~$8.8B (2024)
- Mounjaro: ~$11.5B (2024)
- Zepbound: ~$4.9B (2024)

2025 consensus estimates had Lilly's combined tirzepatide franchise approaching $27–30B and Novo's semaglutide franchise approaching $32–35B, but I should not state 2025 actuals with precision.

**Shortage resolution**:
- **Tirzepatide**: FDA declared resolved **Oct 2, 2024**, then reaffirmed after OFA litigation on **Dec 19, 2024**. 503B grace period ended March 19, 2025; 503A ended Feb 18, 2025.
- **Semaglutide**: removed from shortage list **Feb 21, 2025**, with 503A grace through ~April 22, 2025 and 503B through ~May 22, 2025.

**Consequences for compounders**: The Outsourcing Facilities Association sued FDA in both cases and lost. Mass-market telehealth compounders (Hims & Hers, Ro, Noom) had to pivot to "personalized" compounding defenses under 503A §503A(b)(1)(D), which FDA has signaled it views skeptically. Hims retained a semaglutide compounding offering claiming clinical personalization; enforcement risk remains high. This effectively shuts down the ~$1B+ gray-market compounded GLP-1 channel.

**CDMO network**:
- **Catalent** — acquired by **Novo Holdings for $16.5B (closed Dec 2024)**; three fill-finish sites (Bloomington IN, Brussels, Anagni Italy) transferred to Novo Nordisk
- **Thermo Fisher Greenville NC** — sterile fill-finish for Lilly
- **PCI Pharma Services** — device assembly/packaging
- **Hovione** — spray-dried dispersion API, relevant for oral semaglutide/orforglipron manufacturing scale-up
- Lilly has also committed **~$23B in internal capacity** (Concord NC, Lebanon IN, Research Triangle Park, Alzey Germany)

**2030 market**: consensus range is **$130–150B** global obesity + cardiometabolic GLP-1/GIP/amylin class (Goldman, JPM, Leerink). Upside cases ($200B+) assume CV/MASH/OSA/addiction label expansion; downside cases ($80–100B) assume oral competition and payer gating.

## 3. Biosimilar Wave

**Stelara (ustekinumab)**: US LOE Jan 1, 2025. Launched or approved: **Wezlana (Amgen)**, **Selarsdi (Alvotech/Teva)**, **Pyzchiva (Samsung Bioepis/Sandoz)**, **Otulfi (Fresenius Kabi/Formycon)**, **Imuldosa (Dong-A/Accord)**, **Steqeyma (Celltrion)**, **Yesintek (Biocon)**. All have J&J patent settlements staggering launches through 2025. J&J structured Stelara's "soft landing" via PBM formulary lock-ins (Caremark excluded biosimilars in H1 2025 before partial inclusion). Expect: **Y1 ~15–25% erosion, Y2 40–55%, Y3 65–75%** — slower than Humira due to PBM dynamics.

**Humira (adalimumab)**: US LOE July 2023 (Amjevita first). Erosion was notoriously slow due to Caremark/ESI rebate walls, but the **April 2024 Caremark formulary shift to exclude Humira on commercial template** accelerated conversion. By YE 2024, biosimilar share of adalimumab TRx reached ~**22% by volume but 60%+ by new starts**; AbbVie Humira US revenue fell from ~$18.6B (2022) to ~$5.5B (2024).

**Eylea (aflibercept)**: **Yesafili (Biocon), Opuviz (Samsung Bioepis), Pavblu (Amgen)** approved 2024. Regeneron's Eylea HD (8mg) launch and ongoing patent litigation (preliminary injunctions have slowed launches; Amgen Pavblu launched at-risk in Oct 2024). Y1 erosion likely muted (<15%) due to HD conversion and litigation; Y3 erosion could reach 50%+ once injunctions lift.

**Keytruda / Opdivo**: Keytruda composition-of-matter IP expires **2028 (US), 2030 (EU)**; subcutaneous Keytruda (MK-3475A with berahyaluronidase alfa, BLA 2024-2025) is the defense strategy — target 40%+ conversion before LOE. Samsung Bioepis, Amgen, Celltrion, Alvotech, and Sandoz all have pembrolizumab biosimilar programs in development; I don't know exact clinical-stage dates. Opdivo IP expires ~2028 US; BMS's subcutaneous nivolumab (nivolumab-qcxz, approved Dec 2024 as Opdivo Qvantig) plays the same role.

## 4. US Channel Collapse

**CVS Health**: 2024 revenue ~$373B but margins under severe pressure; Aetna MLR crisis H1 2024, CEO Karen Lynch replaced by David Joyner Oct 2024. Announced **~270 store closures in 2024, 900 total by 2026**. Board reviewed break-up (Caremark / Aetna / Retail) pressured by Glenview Capital; ultimately kept integrated structure.

**Walgreens Boots Alliance**: Sycamore Partners **$10B take-private announced March 6, 2025** (not October 2024 — prompt appears off) at $11.45/share + CVR. Closing expected Q3/Q4 2025. Closing **~1,200 stores** over three years announced Oct 2024.

**Rite Aid**: Emerged from Chapter 11 Aug 2024; filed **Chapter 22 on May 5, 2025**. Selling scripts/assets in piecemeal fashion to CVS, Walgreens, Kroger, Giant Eagle; effectively liquidating retail footprint.

**PBM concentration**: CVS Caremark, Express Scripts (Cigna/Evernorth), OptumRx (UHG) control ~**80% of Rx claims**. **FTC 6(b) interim report July 9, 2024** (not June); **second interim report Jan 14, 2025**; **administrative complaint filed Sept 20, 2024** targeting the Big Three plus their rebate aggregators (Zinc, Ascent, Emisar) specifically on **insulin** rebating. House Oversight hearings July 2024; bipartisan PBM reform (delinking, transparency) attached to multiple vehicles but repeatedly stripped from CRs.

**Rebate compression hotspots**:
1. **Insulins** (Lantus, Humalog, NovoLog) — list-price cuts 65–78% in 2024 post-IRA Part D redesign and ADAP exposure
2. **GLP-1s for obesity** — Wegovy/Zepbound gross-to-net now 50%+ on commercial; formulary exclusions used as leverage
3. (Honorable mention) **DPP-4s and SGLT2s** — rebate walls collapsing as generics/biosimilars loom

## 5. 340B Reform

**Contract pharmacy controversy**: HRSA's 2010 guidance allowed unlimited contract pharmacies; by 2020 covered entities averaged 20+ contract pharmacies, driving duplicate discounts and diversion concerns. Starting **July 2020 (Lilly)**, manufacturers unilaterally restricted contract-pharmacy shipments.

**Rebate-replace models** (2024-2025): Several manufacturers proposed replacing upfront 340B discounts with **retrospective rebate verification** requiring claims-level data:
- **J&J**: Announced Aug 2024 for Stelara/Xarelto; HRSA threatened CMP/exclusion; J&J sued (**J&J v. HRSA**, DDC)
- **Eli Lilly**: Similar proposal
- **Bristol Myers Squibb, Sanofi, Novartis, AstraZeneca, Merck, Boehringer, GSK**: Followed with similar filings/proposals through late 2024/early 2025
- HRSA rejected all; litigation active

**Litigation status** (as of my knowledge cutoff):
- **Novartis/UTHR v. HHS**: DC Circuit **May 2024** ruled for manufacturers — Section 340B does not require delivery to unlimited contract pharmacies
- **Sanofi/Novo/AstraZeneca v. HHS**: **Third Circuit Jan 2023** similarly ruled for manufacturers
- **Lilly v. HHS**: Seventh Circuit, favorable to Lilly
- **J&J v. HRSA**: DDC filed Nov 2024, pending — directly tests rebate-model legality
- I don't know the current status of the rebate-model cases with full precision as of mid-2025

**State contract-pharmacy protection laws**: **Arkansas (Act 1103, 2021 — upheld by 8th Circuit and cert denied by SCOTUS)**, **Louisiana, Mississippi, West Virginia, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Maryland** have passed variants. PhRMA has preemption challenges pending. Roughly **half the states** have introduced similar legislation.

## 6. China API and Inspection

**BIOSECURE Act**: **HR 8333** passed House **Sept 9, 2024, 306-81**. Named entities: **BGI, MGI, Complete Genomics, WuXi AppTec, WuXi Biologics** (WuXi STA and WuXi XDC are WuXi AppTec subsidiaries and thus covered). **Failed to attach to FY25 NDAA (Dec 2024)**. Reintroduced in the 119th Congress (2025); I don't have certainty on current status — as of early 2025 it had not been re-passed as standalone, and attempts to attach to appropriations and the FY26 NDAA were ongoing.

**Contracting timeline** (per HR 8333 text): prohibition on new contracts with named entities from **Jan 1, 2032** grace period for existing agreements; new federal contracts barred 60 days after enactment.

**FDA overseas inspections**: Post-COVID resumption slow. FY2023 foreign drug inspections ~**909 vs. ~1,700 in FY2019** (~46% below). FY2024 improved but still ~**35–40% below** 2019 baseline. China specifically remains most-affected due to visa and access friction; HHS OIG and GAO (GAO-24-106247) flagged the inspection gap as a drug-quality risk.

**API sourcing**: I can give directional figures with caveats — precise sourcing shares are contested because FDA tracks **facilities** not **volumes**. FDA data: ~**13% of API facilities in China, ~18% in India, ~28% in US** for US-marketed drugs. By **volume** of generic API consumed in the US, industry estimates cluster around **China 30–40%, India 25–30%**, with **India sourcing 60–70% of its KSMs from China** — meaning effective Chinese exposure in the US generic supply chain is substantially higher than the direct-import figure suggests. USP and Clarivate have published varying numbers; I would not cite a specific percentage as authoritative.

---

**Flags for CEO discussion**: (i) the 2027 selected list includes Ozempic/Wegovy/Rybelsus as one unit — this is the single biggest commercial variable in your portfolio review; (ii) Walgreens take-private date and FTC report date in the prompt are slightly off and worth correcting before external use; (iii) I've flagged where I'm uncertain rather than fabricate — in particular, 2025 full-year GLP-1 revenue, current BIOSECURE status, and the most recent J&J rebate-model ruling.

Below is the CEO/Head of Commercial view, with explicit confidence levels where facts are still moving. I will be precise where I know the answer and explicit where I do not.

---

## 1) IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

### Statutory schedule
Under the **Inflation Reduction Act of 2022**, CMS is required to select and negotiate a growing number of high-spend single-source drugs:

- **Program Year 2026**: **10 Part D drugs**
  - **Initial Price Applicability Date (IPAD): January 1, 2026**
- **Program Year 2027**: **15 Part D drugs**
  - **IPAD: January 1, 2027**
- **Program Year 2028**: **15 Part D + Part B drugs**  
  - Important correction: it is **15**, not 20, for 2028.
  - **IPAD: January 1, 2028**
- **Program Year 2029**: **20 Part D + Part B drugs**
  - **IPAD: January 1, 2029**

So the sequence is **10 / 15 / 15 / 20**, not **10 / 15 / 20 / 20**.

### First 10 selected drugs for CY 2026
CMS announced the first 10 selected drugs in 2023. They were:

1. **Eliquis** (apixaban) – Bristol Myers Squibb / Pfizer  
2. **Jardiance** (empagliflozin) – Boehringer Ingelheim / Eli Lilly  
3. **Xarelto** (rivaroxaban) – Janssen  
4. **Januvia** (sitagliptin) – Merck  
5. **Farxiga** (dapagliflozin) – AstraZeneca  
6. **Entresto** (sacubitril/valsartan) – Novartis  
7. **Enbrel** (etanercept) – Amgen  
8. **Imbruvica** (ibrutinib) – AbbVie / Janssen  
9. **Stelara** (ustekinumab) – Janssen  
10. **Fiasp / NovoLog** (insulin aspart products) – Novo Nordisk

That list is correct.

### Maximum Fair Price discount magnitude
For the first cycle, CMS disclosed negotiated **Maximum Fair Prices (MFPs)** for 2026. The headline figure widely cited by CMS was that the negotiated prices were **approximately 38% to 79% lower than list price**.  
However, your question asks specifically for the discount **versus net Part D price**.

On that basis, the discounts were **much smaller**. Across the first 10 drugs, the **average MFP reduction versus estimated 2023 net Part D price was in the low-20% range**. I have seen analyses clustering around roughly **20%–22% on average**, though this depends on the methodology used to estimate “net Part D price” because true net is not fully transparent. I do **not** want to overstate precision beyond that.

**CEO implication:**  
- The first-round MFP economics are much less dramatic than the list-price headlines imply.  
- The sharper impact comes from:
  1. **future cycles**, especially if your portfolio is heavily Medicare-exposed;
  2. **commercial spillover / reference pricing behavior**;
  3. **loss of contracting flexibility** and pull-forward of lifecycle decisions.

### “Small biotech” exemption debate
There was a temporary statutory exemption for certain **“small biotech drugs”** under the IRA. In effect, some drugs from companies meeting narrow Medicare-spend concentration criteria were exempted from selection **for 2026, 2027, and 2028 only**. This was always temporary and relatively narrow.  

The policy debate has been:
- whether the exemption is too narrow to meaningfully protect emerging innovators;
- whether it distorts BD/M&A behavior by making companies reluctant to cross thresholds;
- and whether it advantages a tiny subset of firms while doing little for broader biotech capital formation.

### Small-molecule “pill penalty”
This is the more commercially important debate.

Under IRA eligibility timing:
- **small-molecule drugs** become negotiation-eligible **9 years** after FDA approval;
- **biologics** become eligible **13 years** after FDA approval.

That 4-year gap is what industry calls the **“pill penalty.”**

The argument is straightforward:
- It disincentivizes R&D in **oral small molecules**, which are often cheaper to manufacture, easier for patients to use, and highly scalable globally.
- It may bias capital allocation toward **biologics** even where a small molecule would be clinically or societally preferable.
- It compresses the effective commercial window for lifecycle management of oral therapies.

I do not know whether Congress will amend this before 2027 strategy decisions must be made; I would not plan on it.

**Commercial implication:**  
For any oral asset with meaningful Medicare mix, you should assume:
- lower terminal value,
- stronger urgency on launch uptake and indication sequencing,
- and more aggressive pre-eligibility lifecycle work.

---

## 2) GLP-1 supply and access

This area is moving very quickly. I know some points with high confidence and will mark the rest carefully.

### 2025 net revenue: Wegovy/Ozempic and Mounjaro/Zepbound
I do **not know the full-year 2025 net revenue figures**, because as of my knowledge cutoff I cannot verify final audited FY2025 reported numbers. I will not invent them.

What I can say:
- By 2024, these franchises were already among the largest and fastest-growing in pharma.
- By 2025, **Novo Nordisk’s semaglutide franchise** and **Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide franchise** were plausibly each at very large scale globally, but I cannot give you a precise FY2025 net revenue number without current filings.

### FDA shortage list resolution timeline
The broad timeline you cite is directionally right.

#### Semaglutide
- **Semaglutide injection products** were removed from FDA’s drug shortage database on **February 21, 2025**.  
- This was a major event for the compounding market because semaglutide shortage status had been the principal legal rationale for large-scale compounding under shortage exceptions.

#### Tirzepatide
- Tirzepatide shortage status was resolved across **late 2024 into early 2025**.  
- I am not fully confident enough to state a single canonical date because FDA handling and litigation-related implementation timing created some complexity. Your formulation “**removed Dec 2024 / Feb 2025**” captures that ambiguity reasonably well.

### Consequences for 503A and 503B compounders
This matters materially for commercial access and channel dynamics.

Under the FDCA:
- **503A pharmacies** can compound patient-specific prescriptions but generally cannot compound copies of commercially available drugs unless shortage criteria are met.
- **503B outsourcing facilities** can compound in larger quantities, but similarly face limits on compounding essentially copies of approved drugs absent shortage-related conditions.

Once semaglutide and tirzepatide were no longer on the FDA shortage list:
- the legal basis for broad compounding of “copies” became much weaker;
- FDA enforcement risk increased materially;
- large-volume telehealth + compounding models became more exposed;
- many compounders shifted toward arguments around customized dosing, different salt forms, or individualized formulations, but those positions are substantially more vulnerable once the branded product is no longer officially in shortage.

**Commercial implication:**  
As shortages resolve, market demand should re-concentrate toward branded supply and authorized distribution. But affordability and access friction remain, so there is still a residual gray market / semilegal customized market risk if branded coverage remains restrictive.

### Principal manufacturing / CDMO partners
The major named assets/partners relevant to GLP-1 scale-up include:

- **Catalent**
  - Critical fill-finish and device manufacturing capacity.
  - **Novo Holdings announced acquisition of Catalent** in 2024, with Novo Nordisk then gaining access to key Catalent sites for GLP-1 manufacturing support.
- **Thermo Fisher Scientific – Greenville, North Carolina**
  - Important sterile fill-finish capacity in the injectable network.
- **PCI Pharma Services**
  - Involved in advanced drug-device assembly and packaging support.
- **Hovione**
  - Known for **spray-dried dispersion / particle engineering** capabilities; often cited in relation to oral and advanced API formulation support.  
  - Your note “for spray-dried API” is directionally consistent with Hovione’s core competencies, though I would be careful not to overstate the exact product-specific scope unless contract disclosures confirm it.

### Addressable obesity / cardio-metabolic market in 2030
There is no single universally accepted number, but strategic planning should assume an **enormous 2030 market**.

A reasonable executive range:
- **Obesity pharmacotherapy alone** by 2030: roughly **$80B–$130B globally**
- **Broader cardio-metabolic incretin opportunity** including obesity, diabetes, sleep apnea, MASH/NASH-adjacent, CV risk reduction, CKD, and other comorbidity-driven expansion: potentially **$150B+** globally in optimistic scenarios

If you want one board-level planning number, I would use:
- **~$100B obesity market by 2030**
- **~$150B+ broader cardio-metabolic incretin market** if outcomes-based label expansion and supply normalization continue

**CEO implication:**  
This is not just a product class. It is a **system-level reallocation of pharma spend**, especially from:
- traditional type 2 diabetes classes,
- some cardiovascular risk management economics,
- obesity-adjacent specialty care,
- and potentially parts of sleep, renal, and liver pathways.

---

## 3) Biosimilar wave

## Stelara (ustekinumab)
### Launch status
Stelara is now in the middle of a real US biosimilar wave, with **multiple launches beginning in 2025** pursuant to settlement-driven entry dates.

Named products include:
- **Wezlana** – Amgen
- **Selarsdi** – Alvotech / Teva
- **Pyzchiva** – Samsung Bioepis / Sandoz
- **Yesintek** – Biocon Biologics
- **Steqeyma** – Celltrion
- **Imuldosa** – Fresenius Kabi / Formycon
- **Otulfi** – I believe this is one of the ustekinumab biosimilar brand names in the market set; I am not fully certain of sponsor/branding mapping from memory and do not want to misattribute it.

You listed **Steqeyma** and **Yesintek** twice; that appears to be duplication.

The key strategic point is that **2025 is the true opening of the US ustekinumab biosimilar market**, not a single-filer event.

### Commercial expectation
Stelara erosion will likely be:
- slower than old-school small molecules,
- but faster than early-generation biosimilar cases because payers now know how to force migration.

A practical planning range for a major brand facing multi-entrant biosimilars:
- **Year 1:** **15%–30%** erosion
- **Year 2:** **35%–55%**
- **Year 3:** **50%–70%**

For a heavily rebated, pharmacy-benefit-exposed product, downside can be steeper if a payer aggressively excludes originator coverage.

## Humira (adalimumab)
This market is already well into erosion.

- US adalimumab biosimilars entered beginning in **2023**.
- By 2024–2025, **biosimilars had taken well over 60% share in some channel / volume measures**, though exact share differs depending on TRx, units, gross-to-net, and payer segment.
- AbbVie has defended economics with contracting, but the category has undeniably shifted into deep erosion.

This is now the proof point that:
- the US biosimilar market can inflect sharply once formulary incentives align;
- PBM private-label or preferred-product models can accelerate switching.

## Eylea (aflibercept)
US aflibercept biosimilar competition is now active.

Named products include:
- **Yesafili**
- **Opuviz**
- **Pavblu**

These launched in the **2024–2025** window, depending on product and commercialization timing.

Retina is not a standard retail-PBM market, so erosion mechanics differ:
- buy-and-bill economics,
- physician reimbursement spread,
- and clinical conservatism matter more.

As a result, Eylea-type erosion is usually expected to be **slower than Humira**, but once retinal specialists gain confidence and ASP economics favor biosimilars, adoption can become meaningful.

## Keytruda and Opdivo biosimilar pipeline
### Timing

## 5) 340B Drug Pricing Program reform

## Contract pharmacy controversy
This remains one of the most important and unresolved US pricing disputes.

Historically, covered entities increasingly used **contract pharmacies** to dispense 340B-discounted drugs, often through very broad networks. Manufacturers argued:
- the statute does not explicitly require unlimited contract pharmacy arrangements;
- duplicate discounts and diversion risks are inadequately controlled;
- and the program has expanded beyond its original safety-net intent.

Covered entities and HRSA have argued that restricting contract pharmacies undermines access, especially for entities without in-house pharmacies.

## Rebate/replace models
Several manufacturers moved from **upfront discounted replenishment** toward **conditional rebate models**—often called **“rebate-replace”**—for some 340B contract pharmacy claims.

The companies you name are among those associated with these approaches or related 340B distribution restrictions:
- **Eli Lilly**
- **Sanofi**
- **Novartis**
- **Johnson & Johnson**
- **AstraZeneca**
- **Bristol Myers Squibb**

The mechanics generally are:
1. product is sold at a non-340B price initially;
2. covered entity submits claims / data supporting eligibility;
3. manufacturer issues a rebate if conditions are satisfied.

Manufacturer rationale:
- better duplicate-discount control,
- more auditable data,
- narrower coverage of disputed contract-pharmacy claims.

Covered-entity critique:
- administratively burdensome,
- delays cash flow,
- effectively chills use of contract pharmacies.

**Eylea (Aflibercept):** Biosimilars **Yesafili** (Biocon/Viatris), **Opuviz** (Samsung Bioepis/Organon), and **Pavblu** (Fresenius Kabi) entered the market in 2024–2025, though adoption has been slower than Humira due to retinal specialist switching hesitancy and device differentiation.

**Oncology Pipeline:** Biosimilar competition for **Keytruda** (pembrolizumab) and **Opdivo** (nivolumab) is expected post-2028 LOE (Loss of Exclusivity), with Samsung Bioepis, Celltrion, and Amgen developing candidates. No biosimilars are currently approved.

**Erosion Curves:** For immunology assets like Stelara, expect **Year 1: 25–35%** revenue erosion, **Year 2: 45–55%**, and **Year 3: 65–75%** (steeper than Humira due to immediate multi-player competition). For ophthalmology, erosion is slower: **Year 1: 10–15%**, **Year 2: 25–35%**, **Year 3: 40–50%**.

**4. US Channel Collapse and PBM Consolidation**

**Retail Pharmacy Financial State:** **CVS Health** faces margin compression in its retail segment and rising medical costs in its Aetna insurance arm, prompting significant restructuring. **Walgreens Boots Alliance** remains in distress; reports of a **$10 billion take-private transaction by Sycamore Partners** (October 2024) have not closed, and the company continues store closures (1,200 locations announced). **Rite Aid** filed for **Chapter 22** (second bankruptcy) in **May 2025**, accelerating the contraction of the US retail pharmacy footprint.

**PBM Concentration:** Three entities—**CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx**—control **over 80%** of prescription volume, creating oligopsonistic leverage.

**Regulatory Pressure:** The FTC’s **June 2024 interim report** documented PBM rebate practices, followed by a **September 2024 administrative complaint** against the "Big Three" under Section 5 of the FTC Act, alleging anticompetitive rebating schemes that inflate list prices.

**Acute Rebate Compression:** The two therapeutic categories experiencing the most severe rebate compression are **Diabetes/Metabolic** (GLP-1s and insulin, where net prices approach single-digit percentages of WAC) and **Immunology** (TNF and IL inhibitors, where biosimilar entry has forced innovator rebate walls to exceed 70–80% of WAC).

**5. 340B Drug Pricing Program Reform**

**Contract Pharmacy Controversy:** The program’s expansion to multiple contract pharmacies per covered entity (hospitals) has created "duplicate discount" risks (340B discounts stacking with Medicaid rebates) and diversion concerns, prompting manufacturers to restrict unlimited contract pharmacy participation.

**Rebate-Replace Models:** **Eli Lilly, Sanofi, Novartis, Johnson & Johnson, AstraZeneca, and Bristol Myers Squibb** have implemented conditional rebate models. Instead of upfront 340B discounts at the pharmacy, covered entities must submit claims data to prove no duplicate discount occurred, receiving rebates post-dispensing only upon compliance verification.

**Litigation Status:** Federal appeals courts have generally upheld manufacturer rights to modify 340B distribution. In **Lilly v. HHS** (D.C. Circuit), **J&J v. HRSA** (3rd Circuit), and **Novartis v. HRSA** (7th Circuit), rulings in 2024–2025 have prevented HRSA from enforcing mandatory unlimited contract pharmacy obligations, allowing the rebate-replace models to persist.

**State-Level Protections:** **Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and West Virginia** have enacted legislation protecting contract pharmacy arrangements or penalizing manufacturer restrictions, creating a patchwork compliance environment.

**6. China API, BIOSECURE Act, and FDA Inspection Backlog**

**BIOSECURE Act:** The House passed **HR 8333** in **September 2024**. As of early 2025, the Senate has not passed companion legislation; the bill is being pursued via NDAA attachment or appropriations riders. The current text grandfathers existing contracts with **WuXi Biologics, WuXi AppTec, WuXi STA, and WuXi XDC** until **January 1, 2032**, prohibiting new contracts after enactment.

**FDA Inspection Capacity:** Overseas inspections remain approximately **60% below 2019 levels** in 2024–2025, creating significant compliance backlogs for API facilities and delaying approval timelines for new manufacturing sites.

**API Sourcing Dependency:** The US generic drug supply chain sources approximately **40% or more of APIs from China** and **approximately 30% from India**. Critically, Indian API manufacturers rely heavily on Chinese **Key Starting Materials (KSMs)**, creating a nested dependency that the BIOSECURE Act seeks to address without immediate disruption until the 2032 deadline.
